Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

payload.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
payload.holding: The Court held that the multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for fixed/self-employed income based on standardized percentages, and the Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
payload.ratio: In motor accident compensation claims under Section 166 of the MV Act, the multiplier must be selected based on the age of the deceased rather than the claimants, future prospects apply to fixed-salary and self-employed individuals, and appellate courts are obligated under Order XLI Rule 33 and the concept of just compensation to correct and enhance inadequate awards.

payload.court: Supreme Court of India
payload.holding: The Supreme Court held that the principles laid down in Swaran Singh's case regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims, and that a fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
payload.ratio: The decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and does not extend to own-damage claims or disputes between the insurer and the insured where no third party is involved.

As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one. Once it is

In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge:

National Insurance Company Ltd. and Ors. (2005 (9) SCC 174).
The primary stand of the insurance company is that the person driving the vehicle did not have a
valid driving license. In Swaran Singh's case (supra) the following situations were noted:
(i) the driver had a license but it was fake;

(ii) the driver had no license at all;
(iii) the driver originally had a valid license but it had expired as on the date of the
accident and had not been renewed;
(iv) the license was for a class of vehicles other than that which was the insured
vehicle;
(v) the license was a learner's license.
Category (i) may cover two types of situations. First, the license itself was fake and the second is
where originally that license is fake but there has been a renewal subsequently in accordance with
law.
Chapter II contains Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act relating to licensing of drivers driving the motor
vehicles.
Where the claim relates to own damage claims, it cannot be adjudicated by the insurance company.
But it has to be decided by an other forum i.e. forum created under the Consumer Protection Act,
1985 (in short the 'CP Act'). Before the Tribunal, there were essentially three parties i.e. the insurer,
insured and the claimants. On the contrary, before the consumer forums there were two parties i.e.
owner of the vehicle and the insurer. The claimant does not come in to the picture. Therefore, these
are cases where there is no third party involved.
According to learned counsel for the appellants, in such cases the logic i.e. let the insurer pay and
recover from the insured company does not apply.
As noted above, there is no contractual relation between the third party and the insurer. Because of
the statutory intervention in terms of Section 149, the same becomes operative in essence and
Section 149 provides complete insulation.
In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial
one qua the third party.

cancelled by the competent authority. The subsequent renewal of driving license inures the benefit.
In support of his contention, he relied upon a judgment reported in ILR 2002 Kar 1088 in the case
of K G Srinivasamurthy and others -vs- Smt.Habib Khathun and others and 2004 (3) SCC 297 in the
case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. -vs- Swaran Singh and others and sought for dismissal of the
appeal.
9. I have carefully considered the arguments addressed by the learned counsel for the parties,
perused the judgment and award, oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties.
10. The dispute in this appeal is only with regard to liability to compensate the claimants.
11. The occurrence of accident due to rash and negligent driving of Maruthi Omni and the death of
deceased Ramakrishna Hebbar in the road traffic accident occurred on 02.07.2008 are not in
dispute. The defense of Insurance Company is that, as on the date of accident, the driver of Maruthi
Omni was not holding valid and effective driving license. The driving license issued by the
competent authority had expired on 30-04-2008, whereas the accident occurred on 02-07-2008.
Proviso to Section 15 of the Act contemplates that where an application for renewal of license is
made, more than 30 days after the date of its expiry, the driving license shall be renewed with effect
from the date of its renewal. Further, where an application for renewal of driving license is made
within 30 days of expiry, the driving license shall be renewed from the date of expiry. Section 15 of
the Act reads as under:
"15. Renewal of driving licenses.-

hat during
the interregnum period, viz., the date of accident and the date of expiry of license, he did not possess
a valid license, during the prescribed period he could apply for renewal thereof and could have
obtained the same automatically without undergoing a test or without being disqualified. Therefore,
the proviso appended to Section 14 of the Act is unequivocal terms and states that the license
remained valid for a period of 30 days from the date of expiry. If an application is made within a
period of 30 days, the renewal of license will be effected from the date of expiry. If an application is
made beyond 30 days of expiry, renewal is from the date of renewal. In the instant case, the driver of
offending Maruthi Omni got the license to drive the motor cycle with gear from 13-05-1992 to
30-04-1998. Thereafter, he got the driving license to drive the light motor vehicles with effect from
3.4.2002 to 30.4.2008. Subsequently, he got renewed the driving license with effect from
04-07-2008 to 03-07-2014. In the interregnum period i.e., from 30-04-2008 to 04-07-2008, the
driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not holding valid and effective driving license and the
accident had occurred on 2.7.2008. The admitted position is that as on the date of accident, the
driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not having valid and effective driving license. A similar issue
came before the Supreme Court in the case of Ram Babu Tiwari referred to above, whereby the
Hon'ble Supreme Court in para-18 of the judgment has held as under:
"18. It is beyond any doubt or dispute that only in the event an application for
renewal of license is filed within a period 30 days from the date of expiry thereof, the
same would be renewed automatically which means that even if an accident had
taken place within the aforementioned period, the driver may be held to be
possessing a valid license. The proviso appended to sub-section (1) of section 15,
however, clearly states that the driving license shall be renewed with effect from the
date of its renewal in the event the application for renewal of a license is made more
than 30 days after the date of its expiry.

payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.court: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, Madhugiri
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.
payload.ratio: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability.

passages.text:
21) A reading of the proviso to Sub-section (4) as well as the language employed in
Sub-section (5) would indicate that they are intended to safeguard the interest of an
insurer who otherwise has no liability to pay any amount to the insured but for the
provisions contained in Chapter XI of the Act. This means, the insurer has to pay to
the third parties only on account of the fact that a policy of insurance has been issued
in respect of the vehicle, but the insurer is entitled to recover any such sum from the
insured if the insurer were not otherwise liable to pay such sum to the insured by
virtue of the conditions of the contract of insurance indicated by the policy.
(22) To repeat, the effect of the above provisions is this: When a valid insurance
policy has been issued in respect of a vehicle as evidenced by a certificate of insurance
the burden is on the insurer to pay to third parties, whether or not there has been any
breach or violation of the policy conditions. But the amount so paid by the insurer to
third parties can be allowed to be recovered from the insured if as per the policy
conditions the insurer had no liability to pay such sum to the insured.
(25) The position can be summed up thus: The insurer and insured are bound by the
conditions enumerated in the policy and the insurer is not liable to the insured if
there is violation of any policy condition. But the insurer who is made statutorily
liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance
issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third
parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions on account of the vehicle being
driven without a valid driving licence. Learned counsel for the insured contended
that it is enough if he establishes that he made all due inquiries and believed bona
fide that the driver employed by him had a valid driving licence, in which case there

Ltd. v. Cheruva-kkara Nafeessu (supra) referred to above,
the Supreme Court has observed that upon making such payment the appellant can
recover the excess amount from the insured by executing this award against the
insured to the extent of such excess as per Section 174 of the Motor Vehicles Act,

1988 and accordingly, we answer point Nos. 4 and 5 by holding that the insurance
company is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the
conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the amount paid
by the insurance company in view of the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act can be
recovered by the insurance company from the insured before the Tribunal on proof of
breach of condition of the policy.
Point Nos. 6 to 8:
40. It is the contention of the insurance company in both the claim petition Nos. 177 of 1997 and 140
of 1994 that the person who was driving the vehicle at the time of the accident was not holding an
effective driving licence on the date of the accident and, therefore, there is breach of conditions of
the policy requiring that the vehicles shall not be permitted to be driven by a person who does not
hold an effective driving licence. The copy of the insurance certificate issued by the insurer in M.V.C.
No. 177 of 1997 has been marked as Exh. P-6 and the relevant condition regarding the classes of
persons entitled to drive, reads as follows:
Any person including insured provided that a person driving holds an effective
driving licence at the time of the accident and is not disqualified from holding or
obtaining such a licence.
41. The certificate of insurance contains that the policy has been issued in accordance with the
provisions of Chapters X and XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The copy of the insurance policy
has not been produced in M.V.C. No. 177 of 1997. In M.V.C. No. 140 of 1994 the insurance company
has produced Exh.

cified in the policy in respect of any liability which the policy
purports to cover in the case of that person or those classes of persons. If the policy
covers the insured for his liability to third parties, the insurer is bound to indemnify
the person or classes of persons specified in the policy. The same is the effect of
Sub-section (1) of Section 96 which provides that the insurer is bound to pay to the
person entitled to the benefit of a decree he obtains in respect of any liability covered
by the terms of the policy against any person insured by the policy irrespective of the
fact whether the insurer was entitled to avoid or cancel or might have avoided or
cancelled the policy. This means that once the insurer has issued a certificate of
insurance in accordance with Sub-section (4) of Section 95 he has to satisfy any
decree which a person receiving injuries from the use of the vehicle insured obtains
against any person insured by the policy. He is, however, liable to satisfy the decree
only when he has been served with a notice under Sub-section (2) of Section 96 about
the proceedings in which the judgment was delivered...
(21) The Act contemplates the possibility of the policy of insurance undertaking
liability to third parties providing such a contract between the insurer and the
insured, that is, the person who effected the policy, as would make the company
entitled to recover the whole or part of the amount it has paid to the third party from
the insured. The insurer thus acts as security for the third party with respect to its
realising damages for the injuries suffered, but vis-a-vis the insured, the company
does not undertake that liability or undertakes it to a limited extent. It is in view of
such a possibility that various conditions are laid down in the policy. Such conditions,

ty risk becoming unlimited or higher than the
statutory liability. In the case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Jugal Kishore (supra)
this Court observed that the liability under the policy could not exceed the statutory
liability under Section 95 of the Act only on the ground that the insured had

undertaken comprehensive insurance of the vehicle. The payment of a higher
premium on that score, however, did not mean that the limit of liability with regard
to the third party risk became unlimited or higher than the statutory liability fixed
under Sub-section (2) of Section 95 of the Act.
(10) In the facts and circumstances of this case, we find that despite holding the
liability under the policy limited to the extent of Rs. 50,000, the Claims Tribunal and
the High Court were not unjustified in directing the appellant company to pay the
whole of the awarded amount to the claimants on the basis of the contractual
obligations contained in clauses relating to the liability of the third parties and
avoidance clause. However, the Claims Tribunal and the High Court were not
justified in rejecting the right of the appellant company to recover from the insured
the excess amount paid in execution and discharge of the award of the Tribunal.
39. In view of the above said decisions of the Apex Court, it is clear that the liability of the insurance
company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not
inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy and any breach of conditions imposed in the
policy would not bind the third party and the insurance company is bound to satisfy the award
against the third party; and if the insurance company is able to prove that there was breach of
conditions of the policy vis-a-vis the insured and can avoid liability under the policy, it can recover
from the insured, the amount paid by it to the third party by virtue of its statutory liability under the
Motor Vehicles Act.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). The offending vehicle is a commercial truck; the driver held no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing the policy is void. Research supporting and adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, the vehicle was a commercial vehicle (Mahindra Maxi Cab) and the driver had a licence for LMV but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority directly on point. It establishes that even where the driver lacks the proper licence for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not the claimant.
supporting.quote: 'In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required authorisation/badge, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck driver with no valid licence at all — a stronger case for pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The Madras High Court applied the doctrine of 'pay and recover' as recognised by the Supreme Court.
supporting.quote: 'Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent-Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.'

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: A Full Bench of the Karnataka High Court held that under Section 149(1) and (4) MV Act, the insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if a breach under Section 149(2) is proved, and is entitled to recover from the insured. This applies regardless of whether the policy is an Act policy or contractual policy, and even if the breach is 'fundamental'.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is a comprehensive Full Bench decision that squarely addresses the insurer's argument that a fundamental breach (like no licence) absolves it. The court held that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: This directly counters the insurer's likely argument that the policy is 'void' due to the unlicensed driver. The Full Bench held that even if the policy is void under Section 149(2)(b), the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.quote: 'The rule of pay and recover is applicable in view of the mandate in Section 149(4) of the Act and even if there is a breach of the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer is bound to satisfy the judgment and award as if it were a judgment debtor, even if it satisfies the twin tests enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court under Section 149(4)(a) of the Act.'

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class (having only an LMV/transport endorsement), the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all — the principle applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided by pointing to licence deficiencies. The court cited S.Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: 'Reading the provisions of Sections 146 and 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is evidently clear that in certain circumstances the insurer's right is safeguarded but in any event the insurer has to pay compensation when a valid certificate of insurance is issued notwithstanding the fact that the insurer may proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount.'

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy the third-party award even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover. Directly analogous to our facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: Delhi High Court decision that comprehensively reviews the Supreme Court authorities (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided.
supporting.quote: 'Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.'

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant. This is the closest factual match to our case.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even a tribunal-level decision that directly addresses the 'no licence at all' scenario and still orders pay-and-recover. This is the worst-case scenario for the insurer's defence — and they still lose on the liability-to-pay issue.
supporting.quote: 'If the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the respondent No.1 has violated the condition of the policy then direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation since the petitioner is a third party and he cannot be made to suffer due to the fault of the owner of the offending vehicle and same can be recovered by the insurer from the owner.'

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be based on the age of the deceased (not the claimants). For a self-employed deceased aged 42, the multiplier is 14, future prospects addition is 25%, and deduction for personal expenses is 1/3rd for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed/fixed salary — directly applicable. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles: 25% future prospects for age 40-50, multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation. The quantum of ~Rs 51 lakh (as computed) is well-supported by this precedent.
supporting.quote: 'In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years... The selection of multiplier shall be as indicated in the Table in Sarla Verma read with paragraph 42 of that judgment.'

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired on the accident date. The court held the insurer liable. Our case involves no licence at all, but the principle that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties is independent of licence validity is directly applicable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the statutory nature of the insurer's liability to third parties. The court held that even if there is a breach, the insurer pays first and recovers from the insured.
supporting.quote: 'The insurer is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the amount paid by the insurance company... can be recovered by the insurance company from the insured.'

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach does not apply to all cases. However, this case is about own-damage claims (first-party/contractual claims between insurer and insured), NOT third-party claims. The Supreme Court expressly held: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Since our client is a third-party claimant, this judgment actually supports our position by negative implication.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to own-damage/non-third-party claims. The Supreme Court held: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client is a third-party claimant (not the insured seeking own-damage coverage). Therefore, this judgment is distinguishable and actually reinforces that Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims like ours.
adverse.quote: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where passengers carried in a goods vehicle are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered by the policy, the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered. However, this case concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a fundamentally different issue from a third-party road accident victim. Our deceased was a pedestrian/third-party road user, not a passenger in the goods vehicle.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category of persons whose risk is NOT statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. Our deceased was a third-party road user (pedestrian/occupant of another vehicle), whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147(1)(b). The statutory scheme expressly requires coverage of third-party risks. Pay-and-recover under Section 149(4) applies to third-party claims.
adverse.quote: 'In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy (such as gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle), the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149... are not attracted.'

adverse.title: Shivlal And Ors. Etc. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is not liable for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 95 MV Act 1939.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the general proposition that breach of policy conditions can absolve the insurer. However, this case is about gratuitous passengers (not third-party road users) and was decided under the 1939 Act. It has no application to a third-party claimant.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a gratuitous passenger in a tractor (goods vehicle) under the old 1939 Act. The ratio is specific to passengers whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased was a third-party road user — the exact category of persons for whom compulsory insurance is mandated. The statutory scheme under Section 147(1)(b) of the 1988 Act expressly requires coverage of third-party risks.
adverse.quote: 'The insurer is not liable in respect of the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
adverse.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. The insurer may be directed to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that an expired licence = no valid licence = breach. However, the court still ordered pay-and-recover. This judgment actually supports our position that even where the licence is invalid, the third party gets paid.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports our position — the court held that even though the licence was invalid (expired and not renewed within 30 days), the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured. The principle of pay-and-recover was applied, not exoneration.
adverse.quote: 'Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded... the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: Absence of a special endorsement on the driving licence for transporting hazardous goods constitutes a breach of policy conditions entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that breach of licence conditions (lack of proper endorsement) entitles them to avoid liability. However, the court still ordered pay-and-recover, not exoneration. This supports our position.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court in Neelam Devi ordered pay-and-recover — the insurer had to pay the third-party claimants first. This supports our position that the third party's right to compensation is not defeated by licence deficiencies. The only question is whether the insurer can recover from the insured afterwards.
adverse.quote: 'If there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.'

priority_arguments: 1. STATUTORY LIABILITY IS PARAMOUNT: Lead with the principle that the insurer's liability to third parties under Section 149(1) MV Act is statutory and cannot be avoided by pointing to breaches of policy conditions. Cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032), Yallavva (doc_025), and Satto (doc_033).

2. PAY-AND-RECOVER IS THE REMEDY: Even if the insurer proves the driver had no valid licence (a breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii)), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The third party cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach. Cite V.Vijayakumar (doc_035), Chennamma (doc_027), and Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024).

3. SWARAN SINGH APPLIES: The Constitution Bench in Swaran Singh (cited in all the above cases) holds that even where the licence is fake or invalid, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured. Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) expressly limits its contrary holding to own-damage claims only.

4. QUANTUM: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, monthly income Rs 35,000. Apply Pranay Sethi framework: 25% future prospects (age 40-50), multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants). Conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965, funeral Rs 19,965, spousal consortium Rs 159,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 for wife and two minor children per Magma General/Satinder Kaur). Total: ~Rs 51 lakh.
5. NO CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: There is no indication the deceased contributed to the accident. The truck driver's rashness is the sole cause. Do not concede any deduction.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 x 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42 per Pranay Sethi) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965, funeral Rs 19,965, consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 for wife and two minor children per Magma General v. Nanu Ram and United India v. Satinder Kaur). Total: Rs 50,99,650. The upper range reflects the possibility of arguing the deceased was in permanent employment (50% future prospects for under-40, but deceased is 42 so 30% for permanent employment age 40-50).
risks: The insurer will argue that the driver having NO licence at all (as opposed to having a licence but lacking an endorsement) constitutes a fundamental breach that should exonerate them entirely. Counter: Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — even 'no licence' results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.

The insurer may argue that the policy is 'void' under Section 149(2)(b). Counter: Yallavva (doc_025) expressly holds that even if the policy is void, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.

The insurer may challenge the income of Rs 35,000/month. Ensure documentary proof (salary slips, bank statements, IT returns) is available. If the deceased was in informal employment, the tribunal may assess notional income, which could reduce the quantum.

The insurer may argue contributory negligence if the deceased was a pedestrian crossing negligently. No facts suggest this, but be prepared to rebut with the criminal court findings (if any) and the principle that the driver of a heavy commercial vehicle bears greater care.
The insurer may delay payment by appealing the pay-and-recover order. Consider seeking a direction for immediate deposit of the award amount under Section 174 MV Act.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek: (1) declaration that the insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants; (2) pay-and-recover order against the insured/owner; (3) compensation of ~Rs 51 lakh with interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition; (4) joint and several liability of the owner, driver, and insurer.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely exonerated from paying a third-party claimant solely because the driver had no licence. Every relevant judgment in the corpus applies pay-and-recover. This is consistent with the settled position under Swaran Singh.

The corpus does not contain a judgment specifically addressing the 'no licence at all' scenario at the Supreme Court level — the closest is S.Iyyapan (doc_032) which deals with lack of commercial endorsement, and Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) which deals with no licence at the tribunal level. However, the principle from Swaran Singh (cited in all these cases) squarely covers the 'no licence' scenario.

The quantum computation assumes the deceased was self-employed. If the deceased was in permanent employment, the future prospects addition would be 30% (age 40-50) instead of 25%, yielding a slightly higher figure. Verify the employment status from available documents.

doc_041 (the mother of deceased case) applies 50% future prospects for a deceased under 40 in stable employment. Our deceased is 42, so the applicable rate is 25% (self-employed) or 30% (permanent employment) per Pranay Sethi.

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi

payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

other purpose including the construction of a room. Thus, there is a violation of the terms and
conditions of the insurance policy. When it is so, then we are of the view that in the instant case, the
insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation and the owner of the tractor will have to

gravity of the offence. Heinous and serious offences involving mental depravity or

payload.court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Madras
payload.holding: The High Court dismissed the second appeal and upheld the lower appellate court's judgment dismissing the plaintiff's suit for specific performance due to lack of proof of readiness and willingness.
payload.ratio: A plaintiff seeking the equitable relief of specific performance must independently plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract in terms of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act.

The plaintiff who has been successful in his suit for specific performance before the trial Court, but
suffered a reversal before the first Appellate Court, has come before this Court with this appeal. The
parties would be referred to by their rank before the trial court.
2.The case of the plaintiff is that the suit property is an agricultural property, that it belongs to

It is further alleged that on 24.09.1992, the second defendant had sold the suit property under

4.However, defendants 1 to 3 did not enter the witness box and consequently, were set ex-parte by

7.The appeal is admitted on the following substantial questions of law;
"1.Whether in law the plaintiff is entitled to the relief of specific performance of

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). The offending vehicle is a commercial truck; the driver held no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing the policy is void. Research supporting and adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, the vehicle was a commercial vehicle (Mahindra Maxi Cab) and the driver had a licence for LMV but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority directly on point. It establishes that even where the driver lacks the proper licence for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not the claimant.
supporting.quote: 'In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.'

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: A Full Bench of the Karnataka High Court held that under Section 149(1) and (4) MV Act, the insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if a breach under Section 149(2) is proved, and is entitled to recover from the insured. This applies regardless of whether the policy is an Act policy or contractual policy, and even if the breach is 'fundamental'.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is a comprehensive Full Bench decision that squarely addresses the insurer's argument that a fundamental breach (like no licence) absolves it. The court held that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: This directly counters the insurer's likely argument that the policy is 'void' due to the unlicensed driver. The Full Bench held that even if the policy is void under Section 149(2)(b), the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.quote: 'The rule of pay and recover is applicable in view of the mandate in Section 149(4) of the Act and even if there is a breach of the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer is bound to satisfy the judgment and award as if it were a judgment debtor, even if it satisfies the twin tests enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court under Section 149(4)(a) of the Act.'

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy the third-party award even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover. Directly analogous to our facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: Delhi High Court decision that comprehensively reviews the Supreme Court authorities (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided.
supporting.quote: 'Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required authorisation/badge, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck driver with no valid licence at all — a stronger case for pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The Madras High Court applied the doctrine of 'pay and recover' as recognised by the Supreme Court.
supporting.quote: 'Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent-Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.'

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class (having only an LMV/transport endorsement), the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all — the principle applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided by pointing to licence deficiencies. The court cited S.Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: 'Reading the provisions of Sections 146 and 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is evidently clear that in certain circumstances the insurer's right is safeguarded but in any event the insurer has to pay compensation when a valid certificate of insurance is issued notwithstanding the fact that the insurer may proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount.'

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant. This is the closest factual match to our case.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even a tribunal-level decision that directly addresses the 'no licence at all' scenario and still orders pay-and-recover. This is the worst-case scenario for the insurer's defence — and they still lose on the liability-to-pay issue.
supporting.quote: 'If the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the respondent No.1 has violated the condition of the policy then direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation since the petitioner is a third party and he cannot be made to suffer due to the fault of the owner of the offending vehicle and same can be recovered by the insurer from the owner.'

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be based on the age of the deceased (not the claimants). For a self-employed deceased aged 42, the multiplier is 14, future prospects addition is 25%, and deduction for personal expenses is 1/3rd for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed/fixed salary — directly applicable. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles: 25% future prospects for age 40-50, multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation. The quantum of ~Rs 51 lakh (as computed) is well-supported by this precedent.
supporting.quote: 'In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years... The selection of multiplier shall be as indicated in the Table in Sarla Verma read with paragraph 42 of that judgment.'

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Where there is consistent oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record contributory negligence based on assumptions from a site plan. Also, even if the driver lacks a valid licence, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court set aside a finding of contributory negligence based on a police sketch where oral evidence showed the deceased was not negligent. It also applied pay-and-recover for the unlicensed driver. Supports both our liability and quantum arguments.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that (a) contributory negligence cannot be inferred from site plans alone if oral evidence contradicts it, and (b) pay-and-recover applies even where the driver had no valid licence.
supporting.quote: 'Once there is clinching oral evidence before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal that deceased was not negligent while driving his vehicle, the Tribunal cannot hold the deceased responsible for 50% negligence only on the basis of sketch/site plan.'

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired on the accident date. The court held the insurer liable. Our case involves no licence at all, but the principle that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties is independent of licence validity is directly applicable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the statutory nature of the insurer's liability to third parties. The court held that even if there is a breach, the insurer pays first and recovers from the insured.
supporting.quote: 'The insurer is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the amount paid by the insurance company... can be recovered by the insurance company from the insured.'

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited and that a fake/no licence cannot be cured. However, the Supreme Court expressly held that Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims — which is exactly our case. The insurer may try to blur the line, but the ratio actually supports us.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to own-damage/non-third-party claims. The Supreme Court held: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client is a third-party claimant. Therefore, this judgment is distinguishable and actually reinforces that Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims like ours.
adverse.quote: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the proposition that pay-and-recover is not available where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered. However, this case concerns passengers in a private vehicle for hire — a fundamentally different category from a third-party road accident victim. Our deceased was a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147(1)(b).
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about passengers in a private vehicle for hire/reward — persons whose risk is NOT statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased was a third-party road user (pedestrian/occupant of another vehicle), whose risk is mandatorily covered. The court itself distinguished Shamanna's case (where there was no valid driving licence and the victim was a third party) and held pay-and-recover was justified there. Our case falls within Shamanna's category, not Sukumarbai's.
adverse.quote: 'When the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as third party; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of pay and recover.'

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
adverse.principle: Where a tractor insured for agricultural purposes is used for non-agricultural purposes (transporting bricks and iron rods), the insurer is absolved from liability as there is a violation of the terms of the insurance policy.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the general proposition that violation of policy conditions can absolve the insurer. However, this case is about a use-restriction breach (agricultural vs non-agricultural use), not a licence breach. The ratio is specific to the type of breach and does not apply to third-party claims where the breach relates to the driver's licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a use-restriction breach (tractor used for non-agricultural purposes) — a fundamentally different category from a driver licence breach. The settled law under Swaran Singh and S.Iyyapan is that licence breaches in third-party claims result in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. Moreover, this case was decided under the 1988 Act but before the full development of the Swaran Singh line of authority on pay-and-recover for third-party claims.
adverse.quote: 'The tractor was insured only for the purpose of agricultural activity... there is a violation of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy. When it is so... the insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation.'

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue about dependency status. However, our claimants are the widow and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) — clearly dependent. This case has no application to our facts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a major, gainfully employed son who was not dependent on the deceased father. Our claimants are the widow and two minor children (8 and 12) — all clearly dependent on the deceased husband/father. The ratio is inapplicable.
adverse.quote: 'A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased is not entitled to compensation under the head loss of dependency.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where passengers carried in a goods vehicle are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered by the policy, the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered. However, this case concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a fundamentally different issue from a third-party road accident victim.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — persons whose risk is NOT statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. Our deceased was a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147(1)(b). The statutory scheme expressly requires coverage of third-party risks.
adverse.quote: 'In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy (such as gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle), the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149... are not attracted.'

priority_arguments: 1. STATUTORY LIABILITY IS PARAMOUNT: Lead with the principle that the insurer's liability to third parties under Section 149(1) MV Act is statutory and cannot be avoided by pointing to breaches of policy conditions. Cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032), Yallavva (doc_025), and Satto (doc_033).

2. PAY-AND-RECOVER IS THE REMEDY: Even if the insurer proves the driver had no valid licence (a breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii)), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The third party cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach. Cite V.Vijayakumar (doc_035), Chennamma (doc_027), and Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024).

supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.

supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority directly on point. It establishes that even where the driver lacks the proper licence for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not the claimant.
supporting.quote: 'In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover. Directly analogous to our facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: Delhi High Court decision that comprehensively reviews the Supreme Court authorities (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided.
supporting.quote: 'Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.'

supporting.quote: 'Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent-Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.'

supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the third party's right to compensation is not defeated by licence deficiencies. The only question is whether the insurer can recover from the insured afterwards.

adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.

The insurer may try to blur the line, but the ratio actually supports us by negative implication.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to own-damage/non-third-party claims. The Supreme Court held: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client is a third-party claimant. Therefore, this judgment is distinguishable and actually reinforces that Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims like ours.

adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the proposition that pay-and-recover is not available where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered. However, this case concerns passengers in a private vehicle for hire — a fundamentally different category from a third-party road accident victim. Our deceased was a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147(1)(b).

adverse.quote: 'When the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as third party; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of pay and recover.'

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi

adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the general proposition that violation of policy conditions can absolve the insurer. adverse.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue about dependency status. However, our claimants are the widow and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) — clearly dependent. This case has no application to our facts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a major, gainfully employed son who was not dependent on the deceased father. Our claimants are the widow and two minor children (8 and 12) — all clearly dependent on the deceased husband/father. The ratio is inapplicable.

adverse.principle: Where passengers carried in a goods vehicle are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered by the policy, the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct pay-and-recover.

supporting.why_it_matters: This directly counters the insurer's likely argument that the policy is 'void' due to the unlicensed driver. The Full Bench held that even if the policy is void under Section 149(2)(b), the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to satisfy the third-party award even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover. Directly analogous to our facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: Delhi High Court decision that comprehensively reviews the Supreme Court authorities (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required authorisation/badge, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck driver with no valid licence at all — a stronger case for pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The Madras High Court applied the doctrine of 'pay and recover' as recognised by the Supreme Court.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class (having only an LMV/transport endorsement), the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all — the principle applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided by pointing to licence deficiencies. The court cited S.Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant. This is the closest factual match to our case.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even a tribunal-level decision that directly addresses the 'no licence at all' scenario and still orders pay-and-recover. This is the worst-case scenario for the insurer's defence — and they still lose on the liability-to-pay issue.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be based on the age of the deceased (not the claimants). For a self-employed deceased aged 42, the multiplier is 14, future prospects addition is 25%, and deduction for personal expenses is 1/3rd for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed/fixed salary — directly applicable. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles: 25% future prospects for age 40-50, multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation. The quantum of ~Rs 51 lakh (as computed) is well-supported by this precedent.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Where there is consistent oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record contributory negligence based on assumptions from a site plan. Also, even if the driver lacks a valid licence, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court set aside a finding of contributory negligence based on a police sketch where oral evidence showed the deceased was not negligent. It also applied pay-and-recover for the unlicensed driver. Supports both our liability and quantum arguments.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that (a) contributory negligence cannot be inferred from site plans alone if oral evidence contradicts it, and (b) pay-and-recover applies even where the driver had no valid licence.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired on the accident date. The court held the insurer liable. Our case involves no licence at all, but the principle that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties is independent of licence validity is directly applicable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the statutory nature of the insurer's liability to third parties. The court held that even if there is a breach, the insurer pays first and recovers from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement on the driving licence for transporting hazardous goods constitutes a breach of policy conditions, but the remedy is pay-and-recover — the insurer must pay the third-party claimants first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for hazardous goods. The court found a breach but ordered pay-and-recover. This supports the principle that even where a licence deficiency is proved, the third party gets paid.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the third party's right to compensation is not defeated by licence deficiencies. The only question is whether the insurer can recover from the insured afterwards.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. However, the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the insured (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired and was renewed after the accident. The court held the licence was invalid on the accident date but ordered pay-and-recover. Supports our position that even an invalid licence results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the third party's statutory right to compensation is not defeated by licence invalidity. The insurer pays first and recovers from the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited and that a fake/no licence cannot be cured. However, the Supreme Court expressly held that Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims — which is exactly our case. The insurer may try to blur the line, but the ratio actually supports us by negative implication.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to own-damage/non-third-party claims. The Supreme Court held: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client is a third-party claimant. Therefore, this judgment is distinguishable and actually reinforces that Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims like ours.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the proposition that pay-and-recover is not available where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered. However, this case concerns passengers in a private vehicle for hire — a fundamentally different category from a third-party road accident victim. Our deceased was a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147(1)(b).
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about passengers in a private vehicle for hire/reward — persons whose risk is NOT statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased was a third-party road user (pedestrian/occupant of another vehicle), whose risk is mandatorily covered. The court itself distinguished Shamanna's case (where there was no valid driving licence and the victim was a third party) and held pay-and-recover was justified there. Our case falls within Shamanna's category, not Sukumarbai's.

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
adverse.principle: Where a tractor insured for agricultural purposes is used for non-agricultural purposes (transporting bricks and iron rods), the insurer is absolved from liability as there is a violation of the terms of the insurance policy.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the general proposition that violation of policy conditions can absolve the insurer. However, this case is about a use-restriction breach (agricultural vs non-agricultural use), not a licence breach. The ratio is specific to the type of breach and does not apply to third-party claims where the breach relates to the driver's licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a use-restriction breach (tractor used for non-agricultural purposes) — a fundamentally different category from a driver licence breach. The settled law under Swaran Singh and S.Iyyapan is that licence breaches in third-party claims result in pay-and-recover, not exoneration. Moreover, this case was decided under the 1988 Act but before the full development of the Swaran Singh line of authority on pay-and-recover for third-party claims.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue about dependency status. However, our claimants are the widow and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) — clearly dependent. This case has no application to our facts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a major, gainfully employed son who was not dependent on the deceased father. Our claimants are the widow and two minor children (8 and 12) — all clearly dependent on the deceased husband/father. The ratio is inapplicable.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where passengers carried in a goods vehicle are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered by the policy, the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered. However, this case concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a fundamentally different issue from a third-party road accident victim.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — persons whose risk is NOT statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. Our deceased was a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147(1)(b). The statutory scheme expressly requires coverage of third-party risks.

priority_arguments: 1. STATUTORY LIABILITY IS PARAMOUNT: Lead with the principle that the insurer's liability to third parties under Section 149(1) MV Act is statutory and cannot be avoided by pointing to breaches of policy conditions. Cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032), Yallavva (doc_025), and Satto (doc_033).

2. PAY-AND-RECOVER IS THE REMEDY: Even if the insurer proves the driver had no valid licence (a breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii)), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The third party cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach. Cite V.Vijayakumar (doc_035), Chennamma (doc_027), and Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024).

3. SWARAN SINGH GOVERNS THIRD-PARTY CLAIMS: The Constitution Bench in Swaran Singh (cited in all the above cases) holds that even where the licence is fake or invalid, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured. Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) expressly limits its contrary holding to own-damage claims only — it actually supports our position by negative implication.

4. QUANTUM: Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000. Apply Pranay Sethi framework: 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50), multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants). Conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965, funeral Rs 19,965, spousal consortium Rs 53,240 for wife + Rs 53,240 each for two minor children (filial consortium per Magma General/Satinder Kaur). Total: ~Rs 51 lakh.

5. NO CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: There is no indication the deceased contributed to the accident. The truck driver's rashness is the sole cause. If the insurer raises contributory negligence based on a site plan, cite Meena (doc_006) for the principle that oral evidence of eye-witnesses prevails over assumptions from a sketch.
6. INTEREST: Claim interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition. If the tribunal awards lower (7.5%), note that Suman Lata (doc_023) reduced to 7.5% but this was in 2005; current rates are higher.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 x 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42 per Pranay Sethi) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965, funeral Rs 19,965, consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 for wife and two minor children per Magma General v. Nanu Ram and United India v. Satinder Kaur). Total: Rs 50,99,650. The upper range reflects the possibility of arguing the deceased was in permanent employment (30% future prospects for age 40-50).
risks: The insurer will argue that the driver having NO licence at all (as opposed to having a licence but lacking an endorsement) constitutes a fundamental breach that should exonerate them entirely. Counter: Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — even 'no licence' results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.

The insurer may argue that the policy is 'void' under Section 149(2)(b). Counter: Yallavva (doc_025) expressly holds that even if the policy is void, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.

The insurer may challenge the income of Rs 35,000/month. Ensure documentary proof (salary slips, bank statements, IT returns) is available. If the deceased was in informal employment, the tribunal may assess notional income, which could reduce the quantum.

The insurer may argue contributory negligence if the deceased was a pedestrian crossing negligently. No facts suggest this, but be prepared to rebut with the criminal court findings (if any) and the principle that the driver of a heavy commercial vehicle bears greater care. Cite Meena (doc_006) that oral evidence prevails over site plan assumptions.
The insurer may delay payment by appealing the pay-and-recover order. Consider seeking a direction for immediate deposit of the award amount under Section 174 MV Act.
The minor children's share of compensation should be directed to be invested in fixed deposits until they attain majority, per Suman Lata (doc_023) guidelines.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek: (1) declaration that the insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants; (2) pay-and-recover order against the insured/owner; (3) compensation of ~Rs 51 lakh with interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition; (4) joint and several liability of the owner, driver, and insurer; (5) direction for investment of minors' share in fixed deposits.

doc_051 (Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State) — Criminal quashing of economic offences. No connection to motor accident insurance whatsoever.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy vs K.Viswanathan(Died)) — Civil suit for specific performance of a sale agreement. No connection to motor accident or insurance law.
